body:
India distinguishes certain genome-edited plants from conventional transgenic crops

Genome editing can alter a plant's own DNA without leaving an introduced foreign DNA sequence in the final plant. This distinction is important in India's regulatory treatment of selected categories of genome-edited crops.

By an Office Memorandum dated 30 March 2022, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 categories of genome-edited plants that are free of exogenously introduced DNA from Rules 7 to 11 of the 1989 Rules. These provisions require GEAC approval for specified activities involving genetically engineered organisms and products, including import, production, use and environmental release.

What SDN categories mean

  • SDN-1: A targeted DNA break is repaired to create a small sequence change without a supplied repair template.
  • SDN-2: A targeted DNA change is made using a suitable repair template, generally involving a defined small modification.
  • SDN-3: Editing is used to introduce a larger DNA sequence, potentially including foreign genetic material.

The Indian exemption concerns the specified SDN-1 and SDN-2 plants without exogenous introduced DNA. It does not mean that all genome-edited organisms are unregulated. Other applicable research, biosafety, seed-variety and release requirements continue to matter.

The Department of Biotechnology notified Guidelines for the Safety Assessment of Genome Edited Plants on 17 May 2022 and subsequently issued standard operating procedures for regulatory review of SDN-1 and SDN-2 plants in October 2022.

India's first announced genome-edited rice varieties

On 4 May 2025, the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare announced 2 genome-edited rice varieties developed by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR): DRR Rice 100 (Kamala), also described in subsequent ICAR material as DRR Dhan 100 Kamala, and Pusa DST Rice 1.

VarietyDeveloping institutionImportant feature
DRR Rice 100 (Kamala)ICAR–Indian Institute of Rice Research, HyderabadDeveloped from Samba Mahsuri; earlier maturity and improved grain-bearing characteristics
Pusa DST Rice 1ICAR–Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New DelhiDeveloped from MTU 1010; improved performance under saline and alkaline soil conditions

These varieties were developed using CRISPR-based genome editing without adding foreign DNA. Their announcement demonstrates a different technological and regulatory pathway from that of transgenic Bt cotton. Development or announcement of a variety should not be confused with proof that every farmer in India was cultivating it.

Gujarat connection: Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre

The Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre (GBRC) is an autonomous organisation under the Government of Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology. It was constituted through a Government Resolution dated 11 August 2017 and commenced operations on 1 September 2017.

Based in Gandhinagar, GBRC promotes applied biotechnology research addressing healthcare, agriculture, environmental and industrial challenges. Its work includes capabilities relevant to genomics, bioinformatics and other biotechnology-based applications. It also supports a shared research facility for institutions and other stakeholders.

GBRC is a biotechnology research institution, not the national authority that grants commercial environmental-release approval for GM crops. That distinction is important when identifying the roles of institutions in Gujarat and at the Union level.

Prelims focus

  • MoEFCC issued the specified SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption on 30 March 2022.
  • DBT issued genome-edited plant safety guidelines on 17 May 2022.
  • ICAR announced 2 genome-edited rice varieties on 4 May 2025.
  • DRR Rice 100 (Kamala): ICAR-IIRR, Hyderabad.
  • Pusa DST Rice 1: ICAR-IARI, New Delhi.
  • GBRC was constituted in 2017 and is based in Gandhinagar.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Office Memorandum dated 30 March 2022 on SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants, as reproduced in Government of India, Press Information Bureau, New Strain of Rice, 19 July 2022; Department of Biotechnology, Guidelines for the Safety Assessment of Genome Edited Plants, 17 May 2022, and SOP notification reported by PIB on 27 October 2022; Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, PIB release on 2 genome-edited rice varieties, 4 May 2025; Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre, Overview and establishment details, consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's 2022 exemption is specifically linked to SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants without introduced foreign DNA.

title: Genome-Edited Crops in India and Gujarat's Biotechnology Institutions

body:
What makes a cell a stem cell?

A stem cell is a cell capable of self-renewal and of producing specialised cells through differentiation.

Self-renewal means that stem cells can divide while maintaining a population of stem cells. Differentiation means that cells acquire specialised structures and functions, such as those of blood, nerve or muscle cells.

In a multicellular organism, different tissues contain cells suited to different tasks. A nerve cell transmits signals, whereas a red blood cell transports oxygen. Most nucleated body cells contain the same inherited genome, but their functions differ because different sets of genes are active; mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus and do not retain this genome.

What does potency mean?

Potency describes the range of cell types that a cell can produce. It does not measure the strength or medical effectiveness of a treatment.

CategoryDevelopmental abilityExample
TotipotentCan form the embryo and supporting extraembryonic tissuesFertilised egg and certain very early embryonic cells
PluripotentCan form essentially all specialised cell types of the bodyEmbryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells
MultipotentCan form several related cell types within a developmental familyBlood-forming stem cells
UnipotentCan produce a particular cell lineage while retaining self-renewalCertain tissue-specific progenitor or stem-cell populations

Totipotency versus pluripotency

A totipotent early embryonic cell has the potential to contribute to both embryonic tissues and the supporting tissues required for development. A pluripotent stem cell can form the major specialised cell types of the body but does not, by itself, have the complete developmental capacity of a totipotent cell.

Why differentiation is important

As development proceeds, cells normally become more specialised. They respond to signals from neighbouring cells and their surroundings. This produces tissues and organs with different functions.

Stem cells are valuable because they help researchers understand development and offer possible ways to replace damaged cells. However, generating a specialised cell in the laboratory is not the same as proving that it will function safely and effectively after transplantation into a patient.

Self-renewal concerns the ability to maintain a stem-cell population. Potency concerns the number or range of specialised cell types that can be produced. A cell may self-renew without being pluripotent.

Prelims focus

  • Stem cells can self-renew and differentiate.
  • Totipotent cells can contribute to embryonic and supporting extraembryonic tissues.
  • Pluripotent cells can produce essentially all body-cell types.
  • Blood-forming stem cells are multipotent.
  • Potency refers to developmental potential, not treatment effectiveness.
  • Trap: Pluripotent and totipotent do not mean the same thing.

[Sources: National Institutes of Health, Stem Cell Basics, sections I–II, consulted 5 November 2026; National Institute of General Medical Sciences, What Are Stem Cells?, November 2024; NCERT, Science, Class VIII, chapter Cell—Structure and Functions, sections 8.2–8.5 (GPSC Books compendium vol. 30, PDF pp. 91–96).]

pictures.alt: Potency narrows from totipotent to pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent, describing cell-type range rather than treatment effectiveness.
pictures.caption: Stem-cell potency refers to the breadth of cell types a cell can produce.

title: Stem Cells, Differentiation and Developmental Potential

body:
Stem cells can be classified by their source

Stem cells are often grouped according to where they come from or how they are produced. Their source influences their developmental potential, ethical considerations and possible applications.

Embryonic stem cells

Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are pluripotent cells derived from the inner cell mass of an early embryo at the blastocyst stage. They can generate many specialised cell types and are valuable for studying development and disease.

The derivation and use of human embryonic stem cells raise ethical questions, particularly where obtaining the cells involves the use or destruction of an embryo. Research is subject to applicable ethical and regulatory requirements.

Adult or somatic stem cells

Adult stem cells, also called somatic or tissue-specific stem cells, occur in the tissues of children and adults. Many are multipotent. They help maintain tissues by replacing cells lost through ordinary wear, injury or disease.

Hematopoietic stem cells are blood-forming stem cells. They can generate red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets through their specialised descendant cells. They are found in bone marrow and can also be obtained from appropriately collected peripheral blood or umbilical cord blood.

Umbilical cord-blood stem cells

Umbilical cord blood collected after birth contains hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. These can be used for selected blood-forming stem-cell transplants when medical and compatibility requirements are met.

Cord-blood stem cells are not the same as embryonic stem cells. A commercial claim that stored cord blood is a guaranteed treatment for any future disease is scientifically unjustified.

Induced pluripotent stem cells

Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are produced by reprogramming specialised cells, such as skin cells, to a pluripotent state. Their importance is that a mature cell can regain the ability to produce many different specialised cell types under suitable conditions.

Shinya Yamanaka demonstrated successful reprogramming of mature mouse cells into induced pluripotent stem cells in 2006. Earlier, John B. Gurdon demonstrated that specialised cells retain genetic information capable of supporting development. They jointly received the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery that mature cells can be reprogrammed to become pluripotent.

Major research uses

  • Disease modelling: Patient-derived cells may be used to study how particular diseases affect specialised cell types.
  • Drug testing: Laboratory-grown cells can help evaluate the effects of candidate medicines.
  • Regenerative medicine research: Scientists investigate whether suitable cells can replace or support damaged tissues.

iPSCs avoid the need to derive pluripotent cells from embryos, but they introduce other concerns, including genetic stability and the possibility that incompletely differentiated cells could grow abnormally after transplantation.

Prelims focus

  • Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent and originate from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst.
  • Adult stem cells are generally tissue-specific.
  • Umbilical cord blood contains hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
  • iPSCs are produced by reprogramming specialised cells.
  • Yamanaka demonstrated iPSCs in 2006; Gurdon and Yamanaka received the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
  • Trap: Umbilical cord-blood stem cells are not embryonic stem cells.

[Sources: National Institutes of Health, Stem Cell Basics, sections on pluripotent, adult and induced pluripotent stem cells, consulted 5 November 2026; NobelPrize.org, The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2012, press release, sections on Gurdon and Yamanaka; Indian Council of Medical Research, National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, terminology and ethical framework.]

pictures.alt: Reprogramming turns a specialised skin cell into a pluripotent iPSC, which can form many body-cell types. Yamanaka demonstrated iPSCs in 2006.
pictures.caption: Induced pluripotent stem cells are produced by reprogramming specialised cells.

title: Embryonic, Adult, Cord-Blood and Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells

body:
What regenerative medicine attempts to achieve

Regenerative medicine aims to restore, replace or support damaged cells, tissues or their functions. Stem cells are important in this field because some can renew themselves and produce specialised descendants.

Not every regenerative treatment involves stem cells, and not every procedure involving stem cells has proved effective. Treatments must be judged according to their actual clinical evidence.

Established use: hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation

Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (HSCT) is an established treatment for selected blood, bone-marrow and immune-system disorders. Depending on the disease and the patient's condition, it may be considered for certain leukemias, other blood cancers, severe marrow disorders, thalassemia and selected inherited immune deficiencies.

The treatment uses blood-forming stem cells that can establish or restore blood-cell production. Cells may come from bone marrow, appropriately collected peripheral blood or umbilical cord blood. The choice of source depends on clinical circumstances.

Autologous and allogeneic transplantation

TypeCell sourceImportant feature
AutologousThe patient's own cellsAvoids donor-recipient tissue incompatibility
AllogeneicAnother person, such as a compatible donorMay replace abnormal blood-forming cells with donor cells

Allogeneic transplantation requires attention to donor compatibility and immune complications. One important complication is graft-versus-host disease, in which immune cells originating from the donor attack the recipient's tissues. Transplantation also carries risks such as infection and complications related to treatment given before the transplant.

How stem cells and genome editing can work together

Stem-cell treatment and genome editing are different concepts, but they can be combined. A patient's blood-forming stem cells may be collected and genetically edited outside the body. After appropriate assessment and clinical preparation, the modified cells can be returned to the patient to support blood-cell production.

The medicine Casgevy, also called exagamglogene autotemcel, is an example of this combined approach. It uses CRISPR-edited autologous blood-forming stem and progenitor cells. The edit increases the production of fetal haemoglobin in relevant blood-cell descendants, helping address the effects of certain inherited haemoglobin disorders.

The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) first approved Casgevy for specified patients with sickle cell disease on 8 December 2023 and for transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia on 16 January 2024. On 1 July 2026, the FDA expanded the US indications to eligible patients aged 2 years and older. These dates describe US regulatory decisions, not an automatic approval in India.

What remains under investigation?

Researchers are investigating stem-cell-based approaches for conditions involving damaged nerve, heart and other tissues. Such research does not establish routine effectiveness. A treatment that improves an outcome in laboratory cells or animals may fail to provide adequate benefit or safety in human patients.

Prelims focus

  • Hematopoietic stem cells form blood-cell lineages.
  • HSCT is an established treatment for selected blood and immune disorders.
  • Autologous means the patient's own cells; allogeneic means donor-derived cells.
  • Graft-versus-host disease is an important complication of allogeneic transplantation.
  • Casgevy combines CRISPR genome editing with autologous hematopoietic stem cells.
  • Trap: A US FDA approval does not by itself authorise clinical use in India.

[Sources: Indian Council of Medical Research, National Guidelines for Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation, 2021, clinical indications and transplant principles; US Food and Drug Administration, Casgevy, Indications and Approval History, consulted 5 November 2026; US FDA, FDA Approves First Gene Therapy for Young Children with Sickle Cell Disease, 1 July 2026.]

pictures.caption: Blood-forming stem-cell transplantation is used for selected serious blood and immune disorders.

pictures.caption: Casgevy combines ex vivo genome editing with transplantation of the patient's own blood-forming cells.

title: Stem-Cell Transplantation and the Promise of Regenerative Medicine
